title: Reusable workflows and pinning

story: On 14 March 2025, an attacker got write access to tj-actions/changed-files, a popular action used by more than 23,000 repositories. They did not publish a new version. They pushed one commit of their own and moved the action's existing version tags to point at it. From then on, every workflow that said tj-actions/changed-files@v45, or any other moved tag, ran the attacker's code on its next run, with that job's token and secrets. The code printed the secrets into the build log, and on a public repo anyone can read the build log.

Not one of those workflow files changed. The line that said @v45 on Thursday still said @v45 on Friday; only the code behind the name was different. Repos that had written a long commit hash instead of v45 ran exactly the same code as the day before, and nothing happened to them.
hook.question: How do we call code we did not write, whether an action, a whole shared workflow or a container image, so that nobody can change it without us noticing?

read.h: A tag is a pointer, a hash is the content
p: Every git commit has a commit SHA, a 40-character hash that git computes from the commit's content and its history. Change one byte anywhere and you get a different SHA, so a SHA always names exactly the same code. A tag or a branch is different: it is only a name that points at some commit, and anyone who can push to the repo can move it with git tag -f and a forced push. Moving tags is not even unusual. The actions/checkout repo has a workflow whose only job is to move its major tag, so @v7 meant the v7.0.0 commit until v7.0.1 was released, and means the v7.0.1 commit today.

So when you write @v7, you are trusting the owner of that repo, and everyone who ever steals their access, to decide what runs in your job tomorrow. When you pin, you write the full SHA instead, and nothing can change behind it. The SHA is unreadable for people, so fcp keeps the version in a comment after it. GitHub ignores the comment; Renovate, the bot in the last lesson of this part, updates the hash and the comment together when a new version is released.

code.text:
# what fcp writes
- uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1

# what most of the internet writes
- uses: actions/checkout@v7

# how you find the hash for a version
gh api repos/actions/checkout/commits/v7.0.1 --jq .sha

notes.text: The full 40 characters. A short hash is not a pin: many commits can share the first seven characters, and an attacker can create one on purpose.
Whatever commit the v7 tag points at on the day the job runs.
The commits endpoint accepts a tag name and answers with the commit it points at today.

deeper.h: Go deeper: what a pin does not protect
p: A pin freezes the action's own code, but not everything the action does. If the pinned code downloads a script from the internet while it runs, that script can still change; the attack in the story did exactly that as its second step. Prefer actions that do their work with their own code, and read what an action does before you trust it with a token.

A hash must also belong to the repo you name. GitHub can resolve a commit that exists only in a fork of a repo through the original repo's name, so a hash that someone hands you in a pull request deserves a check. zizmor, the workflow checker you meet in the lab, has an audit for exactly this, called impostor-commit, when you run it with access to the GitHub API.

read.h: A whole job, shared: reusable workflows
p: Sometimes you want to share more than one step. A reusable workflow is a whole workflow file that other workflows call like a function. Its on: block says workflow_call, which means 'another workflow starts me', and it declares typed inputs and outputs, much like the props and return value of a React component. The caller is the workflow that uses it: instead of steps, the caller's job has one uses: line with the file's path and passes inputs under with:. Inside the same repo the path starts with ./, and from another repo it is owner/repo/.github/workflows/file.yml@<sha>, pinned like an action.

Three rules surprise people. First, secrets do not flow to the called workflow unless the caller passes each one by name (or writes secrets: inherit). Second, the caller's permissions are a ceiling: the called workflow can ask for less, never for more, and if it asks for more the whole run fails at startup. The comment in fcp's real caller for Byte, our review agent, is a scar from exactly that. Third, a reusable workflow in a private repo can only be called if that repo allows it in its Actions settings.

code.text:
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [review_requested, synchronize]

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: read
  pull-requests: read
  # a called workflow cannot request what its caller lacks:
  # leaving this out made every run fail at startup
  issues: read

jobs:
  review:
    uses: RhinoHealth/byte/.github/workflows/review.yml@48950220713205732f6246b7ebe46b31c77dda64 # byte-v2026.09.28
    with:
      worker_image: ${{ vars.BYTE_WORKER_IMAGE }}
      app_slug: ${{ vars.BYTE_GITHUB_APP_SLUG }}
    secrets:
      byte_app_id: ${{ secrets.BYTE_GITHUB_APP_ID }}
      byte_app_private_key: ${{ secrets.BYTE_GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY }}

notes.text: The ceiling. review.yml in Byte's repo can use these scopes and nothing more.
Byte's review.yml needs to read issue comments, so the caller must grant it here.
Another repo, one exact commit. The text after # is for people: Byte's release name.
vars.* are repository variables: plain settings, not secrets.
Each secret is passed by name. The called workflow sees these two and none of fcp's other secrets.

deeper.h: Go deeper: what crosses the line between caller and callee
p: Only four things cross: the inputs, the secrets you named, the permissions ceiling, and the outputs on the way back. Files, environment variables and the caller's checkout do not cross, because the called workflow's jobs run on their own fresh runners like any other job. If the called job needs the repo's code, it runs its own checkout.

Keep callers thin: the events, the permissions, one uses: line, the inputs and the secrets. Everything that changes lives in the reusable file, so one new pinned hash updates every repo that calls it. Byte's maintainers move the pins in all callers together with one script for exactly this reason.

read.h: A job inside a pinned image
p: A job can also say container: <image>. The runner then pulls that container image and runs every step inside it, with the job's folder mounted in. Whatever the image contains, such as a built program and its tools, is ready without an install step. Image tags move exactly like git tags: node:24-bookworm-slim points at a new image every time Debian or Node ships a fix. Every image also has a digest, a sha256 hash of its content, and image@sha256:<digest> always means the same bytes. So a pinned container: line has a digest, for the same reason a pinned uses: line has a SHA.

Our platform's independent-approval check, the required check that someone other than the requester approved the PR, uses this pattern. Its code is built into an image in the platform's private repo and pinned by digest in a reusable workflow. fcp's job pulls that one image and runs one command. It never checks out the platform repo, so it needs no token to read it, and nothing in the pull request being judged can change the program that judges it.

code.text:
name: independent-approval
on:
  workflow_call:

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: fcp-runner-set
    container: <our internal registry>/ai-agents-checks@sha256:<digest of one build>
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: read
    steps:
      - run: node /app/dist/independent-approval.js
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          PR_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}

notes.text: Only other workflows can start this file. fcp calls it with a thin caller pinned by SHA.
Our own runners, inside the internal cluster, so they can pull from our internal registry.
One exact build of the check. There is no checkout step: the program is already at /app inside the image.
One command. Its exit code is the check's result: 0 is green, anything else is red.

lab.title: Pin everything you call
needs: The gh CLI, logged in; it only reads public repos here
uv, so that uvx can run actionlint and zizmor
lab.goal: See a moving tag with your own eyes, then pin every action, reusable workflow call and container image in a small scratch repo until the checkers are quiet.

guess.q: Your workflow says uses: some-org/some-action@v3, and it worked yesterday. Tonight the owner moves the v3 tag to a new commit. Your file does not change. What runs in tomorrow's job?

options.text: Yesterday's code, because the workflow file is the same.
options.why: The file only holds the name v3. GitHub looks up what v3 points at each time the job starts.

options.text: The new commit, because @v3 is resolved again on every run.
options.why: A tag is a pointer, read fresh on every run. Only a full commit SHA names the same code forever.

options.text: Nothing: GitHub refuses to run an action whose tag has moved.
options.why: GitHub has no idea a tag moved. Moving major tags is even normal practice; actions/checkout does it on every release.

follow.say: Ask GitHub which commit a version tag points at today. This is how you find a hash to pin.
List the newest tags of actions/checkout. Look at which commit v7 shares today, and which commit v7.0.0 has.
Find the two lines in actions/checkout's own workflow that move the v7 tag, so you know this is routine and not an attack.
follow.see:
run: git tag -f ${{ github.event.inputs.major_version }} ${{ github.event.inputs.target }}
      run: git push origin ${{ github.event.inputs.major_version }} --force

follow.say: Read the security advisory from the story, straight from GitHub's advisory database.
follow.see: tj-actions changed-files through 45.0.7 allows remote attackers to discover secrets by reading actions logs.

follow.say: Make a scratch repo with a workflow that uses two actions by tag, and ask zizmor, a security checker for workflows, what it thinks. --offline keeps it from calling GitHub.

follow.say: Add a reusable workflow and a caller that has a typo in its input, then let actionlint compare the call with the reusable file.
follow.do:
cat > .github/workflows/_greet.yml <<'EOF'
name: Greet
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      name:
        required: true
        type: string
    outputs:
      greeting:
        value: ${{ jobs.say.outputs.greeting }}

jobs:
  say:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      greeting: ${{ steps.make.outputs.greeting }}
    steps:
      - id: make
        run: echo "greeting=Hello $NAME" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
        env:
          NAME: ${{ inputs.name }}
EOF
cat > .github/workflows/ci.yml <<'EOF'
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  greet:
    uses: ./.github/workflows/_greet.yml
    with:
      nmae: Dana

  node:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: greet
    container: node:24-bookworm-slim
    steps:
      - run: node --version && echo "$GREETING"
        env:
          GREETING: ${{ needs.greet.outputs.greeting }}
EOF
uvx --from actionlint-py actionlint

lab.build: Pin everything in the scratch repo. In changed.yml, replace @v7 with the hash you found for v7.0.1, and @v47 with the hash of v47.0.6 (gh api repos/tj-actions/changed-files/commits/v47.0.6 --jq .sha), each followed by a # version comment. In ci.yml, fix the input name, and add @sha256:<your digest> after node:24-bookworm-slim. Then run actionlint, run uvx zizmor --offline --persona auditor .github/workflows | grep unpinned, and finally docker run --rm node@sha256:<your digest> node --version to prove the pinned image exists.
checks: uvx zizmor --offline --persona auditor .github/workflows | grep unpinned prints nothing (the auditor persona also checks container images).
Every uses: of an action has 40 hex characters after the @, followed by a # version comment.
The container: line ends with @sha256: and 64 hex characters.
docker run --rm node@sha256:<your digest> node --version prints a v24 version.

solution.text:
# .github/workflows/changed.yml (the two uses: lines)
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: tj-actions/changed-files@9426d40962ed5378910ee2e21d5f8c6fcbf2dd96 # v47.0.6

# .github/workflows/ci.yml (the caller's input and the container line)
    with:
      name: Dana
    container: node:24-bookworm-slim@sha256:a5f4366e834695d5f363b920c104953a535d3a9864d1bdf74566a0ebe01daee5

# your hashes may be newer: always copy them from gh api and docker image inspect

lab.fix: A week later a teammate 'cleaned up' your work: the checkout pin became actions/checkout@3d3c42e # v7.0.1 because the long hash was 'ugly', and the container went back to node:24-bookworm-slim because 'the digest keeps going stale'. Make both edits yourself, run uvx zizmor --offline --persona auditor .github/workflows, and read the two findings. Put the full pins back, and write one sentence for the teammate about why a short hash and a moving image tag are not pins.
explain: Why does a full commit SHA protect you against what happened to tj-actions/changed-files, and a tag does not?
What crosses from a caller to a reusable workflow, and what never does?
Why does the independent-approval check run from an image pinned by digest instead of checking out its code?
lab.done: actionlint is silent, zizmor finds nothing unpinned, and you can explain why @v7 and node:24-bookworm-slim are names, not versions.

check.q: A teammate says: 'We use actions/checkout@v7, and v7 is a version, so we are pinned.' What do you answer?

options.text: Right: a v tag is a release and cannot change
options.why: Tags are pointers. actions/checkout moves v7 on every release, and an attacker with push access could move it too.

options.text: Not pinned: v7 is a tag that can move; a pin is the full 40-character commit SHA
options.why: Only the SHA names fixed content. Keep the version in a comment so people can still read it.

options.text: Pinned enough, as long as the repo is public
options.why: Public or private does not matter. The tj-actions tags were moved in a public repo, and that is what leaked secrets.

check.q: fcp's caller grants pull-requests: read. The reusable workflow it calls asks for pull-requests: write. What happens?

options.text: The run fails at startup, because a called workflow cannot ask for more than its caller grants
options.why: The caller's permissions are a ceiling. GitHub checks this before any job starts.

options.text: The called workflow gets write, because it declares it itself
options.why: If that were true, any shared workflow could give itself more power than the repo calling it intended.

options.text: It runs, and only the write calls answer 403 later
options.why: GitHub refuses the whole run up front, which is why fcp's Byte caller has a comment about it.

check.q: A job has container: <image>@sha256:<digest> and no checkout step. Where does the program it runs come from?

options.text: From the caller's checkout, which GitHub mounts into the container
options.why: Jobs share no files, and this job never ran a checkout of its own.

options.text: GitHub clones the repo into every container job automatically
options.why: Nothing is cloned unless a step does it. The runner starts with an empty folder.

options.text: From inside the image, one exact build named by the digest
options.why: That is the point of the pattern: the program is in the image, and the digest guarantees which build it is.

p: fcp already pins its actions by full SHA with a version comment, and calls Byte's review workflow at one exact commit. The platform follows the same rules everywhere: every action, every cross-repo reusable workflow and every image is pinned, and Renovate moves the pins with a reviewed PR instead of letting a tag move them silently.

The independent-approval check is the clearest use of this lesson: a reusable workflow in the platform repo, called from a thin SHA-pinned caller in fcp, that runs one build of our checks image pinned by digest.

tickets.why: The independent-approval check: a reusable workflow that runs our checks image by digest, with a thin SHA-pinned caller in fcp.
zizmor in every repo, with an unpinned-uses policy: you now know what it looks for and why.
Renovate updates pinned hashes and their version comments together, including GitHub Actions and base images.

words.plain: The 40-character hash git computes from a commit's content. It always names exactly the same code.
To refer to an action, workflow or image by its hash instead of a name that can move.
A workflow file with on: workflow_call that other workflows call like a function, with inputs and outputs.
The workflow whose job says uses: <reusable workflow>. Its permissions are the ceiling for the called one.
The sha256 hash of a container image's content. image@sha256:<digest> always means the same image.
A job with container: <image>, whose steps all run inside that image.

review.q: Pin actions/setup-node at v7.1.0 from memory: which command finds the hash, and what does the final line look like?
review.a: gh api repos/actions/setup-node/commits/v7.1.0 --jq .sha, then uses: actions/setup-node@<40-character sha> # v7.1.0.

review.q: Name the four things that cross from a caller to a reusable workflow.
review.a: Inputs, the secrets passed by name (or secrets: inherit), the permissions ceiling, and outputs back to the caller. No files, no environment variables, no checkout.

review.q: Why do we pin container images by digest even though the tag has a version number in it?
review.a: Image tags move whenever the image is rebuilt, for example with a Debian or Node fix. Only the digest names the exact bytes, so the job runs the same image until a reviewed change moves the pin.

remember: Call other people's CI code by its hash, never by a name: a full commit SHA for actions and workflows, a digest for images.
